Element $\mathrm{C}$: between $\Delta_{i}H_{3}$ and $\Delta_{i}H_{4}$
Element $\mathrm{D}$: between $\Delta_{i}H_{5}$ and $\Delta_{i}H_{6}$

Which of these elements is expected to form the most acidic oxide?
questions.solution:
The position of the massive jump in successive ionization enthalpies indicates the number of valence electrons an element possesses.

For element $\mathrm{A}$, the jump is after the first electron, meaning it has $1$ valence electron (Group 1).
For element $\mathrm{B}$, the jump is after the second electron, meaning it has $2$ valence electrons (Group 2).
For element $\mathrm{C}$, the jump is after the third electron, meaning it has $3$ valence electrons (Group 13).
For element $\mathrm{D}$, the jump is after the fifth electron, meaning it has $5$ valence electrons (Group 15).

Across a period from left to right, the non-metallic character of elements increases. Since non-metal oxides are acidic in nature, the acidic character of the oxides increases across a period. Element $\mathrm{D}$ (Group 15) is the most non-metallic among the given elements and will therefore form the most acidic oxide.

Answer: Element $\mathrm{D}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-IList-II
A. $[\mathrm{He}] 2\mathrm{s}^2 2\mathrm{p}^6$I. Transition element
B. $[\mathrm{Ar}] 3\mathrm{d}^8 4\mathrm{s}^2$II. Inner transition element
C. $[\mathrm{Rn}] 5\mathrm{f}^7 6\mathrm{d}^1 7\mathrm{s}^2$III. Representative element
D. $[\mathrm{Ne}] 3\mathrm{s}^2 3\mathrm{p}^1$IV. Noble gas

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
A. $[\mathrm{He}] 2\mathrm{s}^2 2\mathrm{p}^6$: The valence shell is completely filled ($n\mathrm{s}^2 n\mathrm{p}^6$). It is a noble gas (IV).

B. $[\mathrm{Ar}] 3\mathrm{d}^8 4\mathrm{s}^2$: The last electron enters the $3\mathrm{d}$ subshell. Elements with incompletely filled d-orbitals are transition elements (I).

C. $[\mathrm{Rn}] 5\mathrm{f}^7 6\mathrm{d}^1 7\mathrm{s}^2$: The last electron enters the $5\mathrm{f}$ subshell. These are inner transition elements (II).

D. $[\mathrm{Ne}] 3\mathrm{s}^2 3\mathrm{p}^1$: The last electron enters the $3\mathrm{p}$ subshell. The s and p-block elements are known as representative elements (III).

Therefore, the correct match is A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III.

Answer: A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q: Identify the correct statement regarding Oxygen and Sulphur:
options: Oxygen has $6$ valence orbitals and can form $d\pi-p\pi$ multiple bonds.
Sulphur is restricted to a maximum covalency of four because it lacks vacant $d$-orbitals in its ground state.
Sulphur has $9$ valence orbitals and can expand its covalency to form $d\pi-p\pi$ multiple bonds.
Oxygen has $4$ valence orbitals but can form $d\pi-p\pi$ multiple bonds due to its exceptionally small size.
questions.solution:
Oxygen (Group 16, $n=2$) has $6$ valence electrons but only $4$ valence orbitals (one $2s$ and three $2p$). Due to the complete absence of $d$-orbitals in the second shell, it cannot expand its octet and forms only $p\pi-p\pi$ multiple bonds.

Sulphur (Group 16, $n=3$) has $6$ valence electrons and $9$ valence orbitals (one $3s$, three $3p$, and five $3d$). The presence of vacant $3d$ orbitals in its valence shell allows Sulphur to expand its covalency (up to six) and form $d\pi-p\pi$ multiple bonds (e.g., in $SO_2$ and $SO_3$).

Therefore, the statement regarding Sulphur having $9$ valence orbitals and forming $d\pi-p\pi$ bonds is the only correct one.

Answer: Sulphur has $9$ valence orbitals and can expand its covalency to form $d\pi-p\pi$ multiple bonds.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The atomic radius of oxygen is smaller than that of nitrogen.
Reason (R): Effective nuclear charge increases from left to right across a period.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.solution:
Nitrogen (Group 15) and Oxygen (Group 16) belong to the second period of the periodic table. As we move from left to right across a period, electrons are added to the same principal shell while protons are added to the nucleus. This results in an increase in the effective nuclear charge, which pulls the electron cloud closer to the nucleus.

Consequently, the atomic radius decreases from left to right across a period. Therefore, the atomic radius of oxygen is indeed smaller than that of nitrogen.

Thus, both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are correct, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

Answer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q: Consider the elements Nitrogen (N), Oxygen (O), and Fluorine (F). Which of the following options correctly represents the increasing order of their electronegativity and their first ionization enthalpy?
questions.solution:
Electronegativity generally increases across a period from left to right due to an increase in effective nuclear charge. Therefore, the correct increasing order of electronegativity for these Period 2 elements is $\mathrm{N} \lt \mathrm{O} \lt \mathrm{F}$.

First ionization enthalpy also generally increases across a period, but there is an exception between Group 15 and Group 16. Nitrogen (Group 15) has a stable half-filled $2p$ subshell ($2s^{2} 2p^{3}$), whereas Oxygen (Group 16) has a $2s^{2} 2p^{4}$ configuration. Removing an electron from the stable half-filled orbitals of nitrogen requires more energy than removing an electron from oxygen. Hence, the first ionization enthalpy of nitrogen is higher than that of oxygen. Fluorine has the highest first ionization enthalpy among the three. Thus, the correct increasing order for first ionization enthalpy is $\mathrm{O} \lt \mathrm{N} \lt \mathrm{F}$.

Answer: Electronegativity: $\mathrm{N} \lt \mathrm{O} \lt \mathrm{F}$ ; First ionization enthalpy: $\mathrm{O} \lt \mathrm{N} \lt \mathrm{F}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The oxide of the element with atomic number $11$ is acidic, whereas the oxide of the element with atomic number $17$ is basic.
Reason (R): Across a period from left to right, the non-metallic character increases, which leads to an increase in the acidic character of the oxides.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are correct and Reason (R) is the correct explanation for Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are correct but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation for Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is correct but Reason (R) is incorrect.
Assertion (A) is incorrect but Reason (R) is correct.
questions.solution:
The element with atomic number $11$ is Sodium ($\mathrm{Na}$), which is an alkali metal and forms a strongly basic oxide ($\mathrm{Na_2O}$). The element with atomic number $17$ is Chlorine ($\mathrm{Cl}$), which is a halogen (non-metal) and forms highly acidic oxides (such as $\mathrm{Cl_2O_7}$). Therefore, Assertion (A) is incorrect.

Reason (R) is correct because as we move from left to right across a period, the effective nuclear charge increases and atomic size decreases, leading to an increase in non-metallic character. Non-metal oxides are generally acidic, so the acidic character of oxides increases across a period.

Answer: Assertion (A) is incorrect but Reason (R) is correct.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q: Considering the stability of oxidation states, which of the following relationships is correct for Group 14 chlorides?
questions.solution:
In Group 14 elements (C, Si, Ge, Sn, Pb), the general valence shell electronic configuration is $ns^2 np^2$. They primarily exhibit +4 and +2 oxidation states.

Down the group, the stability of the higher oxidation state (+4) decreases and that of the lower oxidation state (+2) increases due to the inert pair effect (the reluctance of $ns^2$ electrons to participate in bond formation).

For lighter elements like Si, Ge, and Sn, the +4 state is more stable than the +2 state. Therefore, $SiCl_4$, $GeCl_4$, and $SnCl_4$ are more stable than their respective dichlorides.

For the heaviest element, Pb, the +2 state is more stable than the +4 state. Hence, $PbCl_2$ is more stable than $PbCl_4$.

Answer: $PbCl_2 \gt PbCl_4$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
The first four successive ionization enthalpies (in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$) for two unidentified Period 3 elements, X and Y, are given below:

Element X: 737, 1450, 7730, 10500
Element Y: 577, 1816, 2744, 11577

Identify the groups to which X and Y belong, and choose the correct relationship between their first ionization enthalpies ($\Delta_{i}H_{1}$).
options: X belongs to Group 2, Y belongs to Group 13, and $\Delta_{i}H_{1}(\text{X}) \lt  \Delta_{i}H_{1}(\text{Y})$
X belongs to Group 2, Y belongs to Group 13, and $\Delta_{i}H_{1}(\text{X}) \gt  \Delta_{i}H_{1}(\text{Y})$
X belongs to Group 1, Y belongs to Group 2, and $\Delta_{i}H_{1}(\text{X}) \lt  \Delta_{i}H_{1}(\text{Y})$
X belongs to Group 13, Y belongs to Group 2, and $\Delta_{i}H_{1}(\text{X}) \gt  \Delta_{i}H_{1}(\text{Y})$
questions.solution:
Analyze the successive ionization enthalpies to find the number of valence electrons:

For element X, there is a sudden large jump between the second ($1450 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) and third ($7730 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) ionization enthalpies. This indicates that X has 2 valence electrons, so it belongs to Group 2 (Magnesium).

For element Y, the large jump occurs between the third ($2744 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) and fourth ($11577 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) ionization enthalpies. This indicates that Y has 3 valence electrons, so it belongs to Group 13 (Aluminium).

Comparing their first ionization enthalpies: Element X (Mg) has a stable, fully filled 3s subshell ($3s^{2}$), whereas element Y (Al) has a $3s^{2} 3p^{1}$ configuration. The 3s electrons are more penetrating and tightly bound to the nucleus than the 3p electron. Therefore, it requires more energy to remove an electron from X than from Y.

Thus, X is in Group 2, Y is in Group 13, and $\Delta_{i}H_{1}(\text{X}) \gt \Delta_{i}H_{1}(\text{Y})$.

Answer: X belongs to Group 2, Y belongs to Group 13, and $\Delta_{i}H_{1}(\text{X}) \gt \Delta_{i}H_{1}(\text{Y})$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q: Based on the stability of oxidation states dictated by the inert pair effect, which of the following redox reactions is thermodynamically most feasible?
questions.solution:
Due to the inert pair effect, the stability of the lower oxidation state increases down the group for p-block elements.

In Group 14, the $+4$ oxidation state is more stable for lighter elements like Sn, while the $+2$ oxidation state is more stable for the heaviest element Pb. Therefore, $\text{Sn}^{2+}$ tends to oxidize to $\text{Sn}^{4+}$ (acting as a reducing agent), and $\text{Pb}^{4+}$ tends to reduce to $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ (acting as an oxidizing agent).

Thus, the reaction $\text{Sn}^{2+} + \text{Pb}^{4+} \rightarrow \text{Sn}^{4+} + \text{Pb}^{2+}$ is highly feasible as both elements proceed towards their most stable oxidation states.

In contrast, $\text{Tl}^{+}$ and $\text{In}^{3+}$ are already in their stable states, as are $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ and $\text{Ge}^{4+}$, making their respective reactions non-feasible.

Answer: $\text{Sn}^{2+} + \text{Pb}^{4+} \rightarrow \text{Sn}^{4+} + \text{Pb}^{2+}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The first ionization enthalpy of oxygen is less than that of nitrogen, but the second ionization enthalpy of oxygen is greater than that of nitrogen.

Reason (R): The atomic radius of oxygen is smaller than that of nitrogen.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is true: The first ionization enthalpy of nitrogen ($2s^2 2p^3$) is higher than that of oxygen ($2s^2 2p^4$) due to the extra stability of the exactly half-filled $2p$ subshell in nitrogen. However, after removing one electron, the oxygen cation ($\text{O}^+$) acquires a stable half-filled $2p^3$ configuration, while the nitrogen cation ($\text{N}^+$) has a $2p^2$ configuration. Thus, removing a second electron is harder for oxygen, making its second ionization enthalpy greater than that of nitrogen.

Reason (R) is true: Atomic radius generally decreases from left to right across a period, so oxygen is smaller than nitrogen.

However, Reason (R) is not the correct explanation for Assertion (A). The smaller size of oxygen would normally imply a higher first ionization enthalpy, which contradicts the actual trend. The correct explanation lies in the stability of the electronic configurations (half-filled $p$-orbitals), not the atomic radius.

Therefore, both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

Answer: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Element)List-II (First ionization enthalpy in $\mathrm{kJ \ mol^{-1}}$)
(A) Boron(I) $1402$
(B) Carbon(II) $1314$
(C) Nitrogen(III) $1086$
(D) Oxygen(IV) $801$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
The general trend across a period is an increase in first ionization enthalpy due to increasing effective nuclear charge. However, Nitrogen ($\mathrm{N}$, $2s^2 2p^3$) has a higher first ionization enthalpy than Oxygen ($\mathrm{O}$, $2s^2 2p^4$) because of the extra stability associated with its exactly half-filled $2p$ subshell.

Thus, the correct increasing order of first ionization enthalpy is $\mathrm{B} \lt \mathrm{C} \lt \mathrm{O} \lt \mathrm{N}$.

Arranging the given numerical values in increasing order: $801 \lt 1086 \lt 1314 \lt 1402 \ \mathrm{kJ \ mol^{-1}}$.

Matching the elements to these values:
Boron ($\mathrm{B}$) = $801 \ \mathrm{kJ \ mol^{-1}}$ (IV)
Carbon ($\mathrm{C}$) = $1086 \ \mathrm{kJ \ mol^{-1}}$ (III)
Oxygen ($\mathrm{O}$) = $1314 \ \mathrm{kJ \ mol^{-1}}$ (II)
Nitrogen ($\mathrm{N}$) = $1402 \ \mathrm{kJ \ mol^{-1}}$ (I)

Therefore, the correct match is (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(II).

Answer: (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q: Which of the following represents the correct decreasing order of negative electron gain enthalpy for the elements of Group 16?
questions.solution:
In Group 16, the negative electron gain enthalpy generally decreases (becomes less negative) down the group as atomic size increases.

However, oxygen has a significantly smaller atomic size than sulfur. The addition of an electron to the compact $2p$ subshell of oxygen results in strong interelectronic repulsions. As a result, the incoming electron feels less attraction from the nucleus, making the electron gain enthalpy of oxygen the least negative in the entire group.

Thus, the correct decreasing order of negative electron gain enthalpy is $\text{S} \gt \text{Se} \gt \text{Te} \gt \text{O}$.

Answer: $\text{S} \gt \text{Se} \gt \text{Te} \gt \text{O}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q: Which of the following electronic configurations represents a d-block element belonging to the 5th period?
questions.solution:
The period of an element is given by the highest principal quantum number ($n$) of its valence shell.

$[\mathrm{Kr}] 4\mathrm{d}^5 5\mathrm{s}^1$: The highest principal quantum number is $n=5$, so it belongs to the 5th period. The last electron enters the $4\mathrm{d}$ subshell, making it a d-block element. This is the correct configuration.

$[\mathrm{Ar}] 3\mathrm{d}^{10} 4\mathrm{s}^2 4\mathrm{p}^3$: The highest principal quantum number is $n=4$ (4th period) and the last electron enters the $4\mathrm{p}$ subshell (p-block).

$[\mathrm{Xe}] 4\mathrm{f}^{14} 5\mathrm{d}^2 6\mathrm{s}^2$: The highest principal quantum number is $n=6$ (6th period) and it is a d-block element.

$[\mathrm{Kr}] 5\mathrm{s}^2$: The highest principal quantum number is $n=5$ (5th period) but the last electron enters the $5\mathrm{s}$ subshell, making it an s-block element.

Answer: $[\mathrm{Kr}] 4\mathrm{d}^5 5\mathrm{s}^1$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Read the following statements carefully:

(I) Atomic radius strictly decreases from left to right across the entire second period.
(II) A cation is always smaller than its parent atom.
(III) An anion is always larger than its parent atom.
(IV) Among isoelectronic species, the ionic radius increases with an increase in nuclear charge.

How many of the above statements are correct?
questions.solution:
Let us evaluate each statement based on periodic trends:

Statement (I) is incorrect. While atomic radius generally decreases across a period due to increasing effective nuclear charge, noble gases at the end of the period (like Neon) are an exception. Their non-bonded (van der Waals) radii are measured, which are significantly larger than the covalent radii of the preceding halogens.

Statement (II) is correct. A cation is formed by the loss of electrons, which increases the effective nuclear charge per electron, pulling the remaining electrons closer to the nucleus.

Statement (III) is correct. An anion is formed by gaining electrons, which increases electron-electron repulsion and decreases the effective nuclear charge, causing the electron cloud to expand.

Statement (IV) is incorrect. For isoelectronic species (which have the same number of electrons), a higher nuclear charge (more protons) exerts a stronger pull on the electrons, resulting in a smaller ionic radius.

Thus, exactly two statements (II and III) are correct.

Answer: 2

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Match List I with List II.

List IList II
(A) Element with the most negative electron gain enthalpy(I) $\mathrm{Na}$
(B) Element with the lowest first ionization enthalpy in Period 3(II) $\mathrm{K}^{+}$
(C) Cation which is isoelectronic with Argon(III) $\mathrm{Cs}$
(D) Alkali metal with the largest atomic radius(IV) $\mathrm{Cl}$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
(A) Chlorine ($\mathrm{Cl}$) has the most negative electron gain enthalpy among all elements due to its relatively larger size than fluorine, which reduces interelectronic repulsions.

(B) Sodium ($\mathrm{Na}$) is an alkali metal and has the largest atomic size in Period 3, resulting in the lowest first ionization enthalpy in that period.

(C) Argon ($\mathrm{Ar}$) has 18 electrons. The potassium cation ($\mathrm{K}^{+}$) also has $19 - 1 = 18$ electrons, making them isoelectronic.

(D) Caesium ($\mathrm{Cs}$) is the alkali metal with the largest atomic radius (excluding the radioactive francium) because atomic radius increases down the group as new shells are added.

Therefore, the correct matching is (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(III).

Answer: (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(III)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Element)List-II (Properties)
A. BoronI. $3$ valence electrons, $9$ valence orbitals
B. AluminiumII. $5$ valence electrons, $4$ valence orbitals
C. NitrogenIII. $3$ valence electrons, $4$ valence orbitals
D. PhosphorusIV. $5$ valence electrons, $9$ valence orbitals

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Boron (Group 13, $n=2$) has $3$ valence electrons ($2s^2 2p^1$). Its valence shell has one $2s$ and three $2p$ orbitals, giving a total of $4$ valence orbitals.

Aluminium (Group 13, $n=3$) has $3$ valence electrons ($3s^2 3p^1$). Its valence shell includes one $3s$, three $3p$, and five $3d$ orbitals, giving a total of $9$ valence orbitals.

Nitrogen (Group 15, $n=2$) has $5$ valence electrons ($2s^2 2p^3$) and $4$ valence orbitals.

Phosphorus (Group 15, $n=3$) has $5$ valence electrons ($3s^2 3p^3$) and $9$ valence orbitals.

Students often confuse valence electrons with valence orbitals, or forget that empty $d$-orbitals in the third period count towards the total valence orbitals.

Answer: A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Antimony(V) oxide ($Sb_2O_5$) is a stronger oxidizing agent than bismuth(V) oxide ($Bi_2O_5$).
Reason (R): The stability of the +5 oxidation state decreases and that of the +3 state increases down Group 15 due to the inert pair effect.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.solution:
Bismuth (Bi) is the heaviest element in Group 15. Due to the strong inert pair effect, the $ns^2$ electrons in Bi are reluctant to participate in bonding, making its +3 oxidation state much more stable than its +5 state.

Because the +5 state of Bi is highly unstable, compounds like $Bi_2O_5$ readily accept electrons to get reduced to the more stable +3 state ($Bi_2O_3$). This makes $Bi_2O_5$ a very strong oxidizing agent, much stronger than $Sb_2O_5$. Therefore, Assertion (A) is false.

The Reason (R) correctly states the general trend for Group 15 elements: the stability of the lower oxidation state (+3) increases and the higher oxidation state (+5) decreases down the group due to the inert pair effect. Thus, Reason (R) is true.

Answer: (A) is false but (R) is true

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Successive Ionization Enthalpies in kJ mol$^{-1}$)List-II (Classification)
(P) $\text{IE}_1 = 520, \text{IE}_2 = 7300, \text{IE}_3 = 11815$(i) Reactive non-metal
(Q) $\text{IE}_1 = 2372, \text{IE}_2 = 5251, \text{IE}_3 = 6280$(ii) Noble gas
(R) $\text{IE}_1 = 1681, \text{IE}_2 = 3374, \text{IE}_3 = 6050$(iii) Alkali metal
(S) $\text{IE}_1 = 900, \text{IE}_2 = 1757, \text{IE}_3 = 14848$(iv) Alkaline earth metal

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
The difference between successive ionization enthalpies helps identify the number of valence electrons and the chemical nature of the element.

For P: There is a massive jump between $\text{IE}_1$ and $\text{IE}_2$ (from $520$ to $7300\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$). This indicates the removal of the second electron disrupts a stable noble gas core. Thus, P has 1 valence electron and is an Alkali metal (iii).

For Q: The first ionization enthalpy is exceptionally high ($2372\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) with no sudden proportional jump in the first three values. This is characteristic of a Noble gas (ii) with a highly stable closed-shell configuration.

For R: The $\text{IE}_1$ is high ($1681\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) but lower than that of Q, and the successive values increase steadily without an extreme jump. This indicates a Reactive non-metal (i), such as a halogen, which has high ionization energy but does not lose its core electrons in the first few ionizations.

For S: There is a massive jump between $\text{IE}_2$ and $\text{IE}_3$ (from $1757$ to $14848\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$). This indicates the element has 2 valence electrons and is an Alkaline earth metal (iv).

Therefore, the correct matching is (P)-(iii), (Q)-(ii), (R)-(i), (S)-(iv).

Answer: (P)-(iii), (Q)-(ii), (R)-(i), (S)-(iv)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q: The sum of the first two ionisation enthalpies $(IE_1 + IE_2)$ for nickel (Ni) is less than that for platinum (Pt). However, the sum of the first four ionisation enthalpies $(IE_1 + IE_2 + IE_3 + IE_4)$ for platinum is less than that for nickel. Based on this data, which of the following statements regarding the thermodynamic stability of their compounds is correct?
options: $\text{Pt}^{2+}$ compounds are more stable than $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ compounds, and $\text{Ni}^{4+}$ compounds are more stable than $\text{Pt}^{4+}$ compounds.
Both $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ and $\text{Ni}^{4+}$ compounds are more stable than the corresponding platinum compounds.
Both $\text{Pt}^{2+}$ and $\text{Pt}^{4+}$ compounds are more stable than the corresponding nickel compounds.
$\text{Ni}^{2+}$ compounds are more stable than $\text{Pt}^{2+}$ compounds, and $\text{Pt}^{4+}$ compounds are more stable than $\text{Ni}^{4+}$ compounds.
questions.solution:
The thermodynamic stability of a particular oxidation state of a transition metal can be evaluated using the sum of the relevant ionisation enthalpies. A lower sum of ionisation enthalpies implies that less energy is required to reach that oxidation state, resulting in higher thermodynamic stability.

Since the sum of the first two ionisation enthalpies $(IE_1 + IE_2)$ for Ni is less than that for Pt, it requires less energy to form $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ compared to $\text{Pt}^{2+}$. Thus, $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ compounds are thermodynamically more stable than $\text{Pt}^{2+}$ compounds.

Conversely, the sum of the first four ionisation enthalpies $(IE_1 + IE_2 + IE_3 + IE_4)$ for Pt is less than that for Ni. This means it requires less energy to form $\text{Pt}^{4+}$ compared to $\text{Ni}^{4+}$. Therefore, $\text{Pt}^{4+}$ compounds are more stable than $\text{Ni}^{4+}$ compounds.

Answer: $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ compounds are more stable than $\text{Pt}^{2+}$ compounds, and $\text{Pt}^{4+}$ compounds are more stable than $\text{Ni}^{4+}$ compounds.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The negative electron gain enthalpy of fluorine is greater than that of chlorine because fluorine is more electronegative.
Reason (R): Due to the small size of the fluorine atom, there are strong interelectronic repulsions in its relatively compact $2p$ subshell.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is incorrect. Although fluorine is the most electronegative element, its negative electron gain enthalpy is actually less than that of chlorine. This is a well-known exception in the periodic table.

Reason (R) is correct. The reason for this anomaly is that the fluorine atom is very small, and its $2p$ subshell is compact. When an incoming electron is added to the $2p$ orbitals of fluorine, it experiences strong interelectronic repulsions from the existing electrons, making the addition of the electron less energetically favourable compared to adding an electron to the larger $3p$ subshell of chlorine.

Therefore, (A) is not correct but (R) is correct.

Answer: (A) is not correct but (R) is correct

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q: What is the maximum covalency and the total number of valence orbitals, respectively, for a nitrogen atom?
questions.solution:
Nitrogen (atomic number $7$) belongs to the second period ($n=2$).

Its electronic configuration is $1s^{2} 2s^{2} 2p^{3}$. The valence shell is the second shell, which contains one $2s$ orbital and three $2p$ orbitals. Thus, the total number of valence orbitals is $4$.

Because there are no $d$-orbitals in the second principal shell, nitrogen cannot expand its octet. Therefore, its maximum covalency is strictly limited to $4$ (for example, in the ammonium ion, $[NH_{4}]^{+}$).

Nitrogen has $5$ valence electrons and a common ground-state valency of $3$, but its maximum covalency is $4$.

Answer: $4$ and $4$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Element X ($\text{IE}_1 = 495\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$, $\text{IE}_2 = 4562\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) is more metallic and forms a more basic oxide than Element Y ($\text{IE}_1 = 737\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$, $\text{IE}_2 = 1450\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$, $\text{IE}_3 = 7732\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) which belongs to the same period.

Reason (R): The large jump between the first and second ionization enthalpies of X indicates that it belongs to Group 2 of the periodic table.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are correct but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is correct but Reason is incorrect.
Assertion is incorrect but Reason is correct.
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is correct: For element X, the massive jump between $\text{IE}_1$ and $\text{IE}_2$ ($495$ to $4562\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) indicates it has 1 valence electron, so it belongs to Group 1 (alkali metals). For element Y, the massive jump is between $\text{IE}_2$ and $\text{IE}_3$ ($1450$ to $7732\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$), indicating it has 2 valence electrons, so it belongs to Group 2 (alkaline earth metals). In a given period, Group 1 elements have larger atomic radii and lower effective nuclear charge than Group 2 elements, making them more metallic and their oxides more basic.

Reason (R) is incorrect: The large jump between the first and second ionization enthalpies of X indicates the removal of the second electron breaks a stable noble gas core. This means X has only one valence electron and belongs to Group 1, not Group 2.

Answer: Assertion is correct but Reason is incorrect.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The first ionization enthalpy of Magnesium is greater than that of Aluminium, but the second ionization enthalpy of Magnesium is lower than that of Aluminium.

Reason (R): The valence electron configuration of $\mathrm{Mg}$ is $3s^{2}$ and that of $\mathrm{Al}$ is $3s^{2} 3p^{1}$, whereas their univalent cations $\mathrm{Mg}^{+}$ and $\mathrm{Al}^{+}$ have $3s^{1}$ and $3s^{2}$ configurations respectively.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is true: The first ionization enthalpy of $\mathrm{Mg}$ is greater than that of $\mathrm{Al}$. However, the second ionization enthalpy of $\mathrm{Mg}$ is lower than that of $\mathrm{Al}$.

Reason (R) is true and correctly explains (A): The first electron in $\mathrm{Mg}$ is removed from a fully filled and more penetrating $3s$ orbital ($3s^{2}$), requiring more energy than the removal of the $3p^{1}$ electron in $\mathrm{Al}$. For the second ionization, the electron is removed from $\mathrm{Mg}^{+}$ ($3s^{1}$) and $\mathrm{Al}^{+}$ ($3s^{2}$). Because $\mathrm{Al}^{+}$ has acquired a stable fully filled $3s^{2}$ configuration, removing an electron from it requires significantly more energy than removing the $3s^{1}$ electron from $\mathrm{Mg}^{+}$.

Answer: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q: Consider the second ionisation enthalpies ($IE_2$) of the first transition series elements. Which of the following represents the correct increasing order of $IE_2$ for the elements Cr, Mn, Cu, and Zn?
questions.solution:
The second ionisation enthalpy ($IE_2$) involves the removal of an electron from the univalent cation ($M^+$).

The electronic configurations of the univalent cations are:
$\text{Cr}^+ (Z=24) : [\text{Ar}] 3d^5$
$\text{Mn}^+ (Z=25) : [\text{Ar}] 3d^5 4s^1$
$\text{Cu}^+ (Z=29) : [\text{Ar}] 3d^{10}$
$\text{Zn}^+ (Z=30) : [\text{Ar}] 3d^{10} 4s^1$

Removing an electron from $\text{Cr}^+$ and $\text{Cu}^+$ requires breaking the extra stability of exactly half-filled ($3d^5$) and fully-filled ($3d^{10}$) configurations, respectively. In contrast, removing an electron from $\text{Mn}^+$ and $\text{Zn}^+$ involves the loss of a $4s$ electron to achieve these stable configurations, which requires comparatively less energy.

Thus, $IE_2(\text{Cr}) \gt IE_2(\text{Mn})$ and $IE_2(\text{Cu}) \gt IE_2(\text{Zn})$.

Furthermore, due to the general increase in effective nuclear charge across the series, the $IE_2$ values of Cu and Zn are significantly higher than those of Cr and Mn.

Therefore, the correct increasing order is $\text{Mn} \lt \text{Cr} \lt \text{Zn} \lt \text{Cu}$.

Answer: $\text{Mn} \lt \text{Cr} \lt \text{Zn} \lt \text{Cu}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the trends in electronegativity of elements:
I. $\mathrm{Li} \lt \mathrm{Be} \lt \mathrm{B} \lt \mathrm{C}$
II. $\mathrm{F} \gt \mathrm{Cl} \gt \mathrm{Br} \gt \mathrm{I}$
III. $\mathrm{Si} \gt \mathrm{P} \gt \mathrm{S} \gt \mathrm{Cl}$
IV. $\mathrm{O} \gt \mathrm{S} \gt \mathrm{Se} \gt \mathrm{Te}$

How many of the given statements are correct?
questions.solution:
Electronegativity generally increases across a period from left to right and decreases down a group from top to bottom.

Statement I is correct: $\mathrm{Li}$, $\mathrm{Be}$, $\mathrm{B}$, and $\mathrm{C}$ belong to Period 2. Their electronegativity increases from left to right ($\mathrm{Li} \lt \mathrm{Be} \lt \mathrm{B} \lt \mathrm{C}$).

Statement II is correct: $\mathrm{F}$, $\mathrm{Cl}$, $\mathrm{Br}$, and $\mathrm{I}$ belong to Group 17. Their electronegativity decreases down the group ($\mathrm{F} \gt \mathrm{Cl} \gt \mathrm{Br} \gt \mathrm{I}$).

Statement III is incorrect: $\mathrm{Si}$, $\mathrm{P}$, $\mathrm{S}$, and $\mathrm{Cl}$ belong to Period 3. Their electronegativity should increase from left to right, making the correct order $\mathrm{Si} \lt \mathrm{P} \lt \mathrm{S} \lt \mathrm{Cl}$.

Statement IV is correct: $\mathrm{O}$, $\mathrm{S}$, $\mathrm{Se}$, and $\mathrm{Te}$ belong to Group 16. Their electronegativity decreases down the group ($\mathrm{O} \gt \mathrm{S} \gt \mathrm{Se} \gt \mathrm{Te}$).

Therefore, exactly 3 statements (I, II, and IV) are correct.

Answer: 3

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q: Which of the following statements regarding the ionisation enthalpies of transition elements is incorrect?
options: The successive addition of electrons to the inner $(n-1)d$ orbitals decreases the shielding of outer $ns$ electrons, causing a sharp increase in ionisation enthalpy.
The first ionisation enthalpy generally increases along a transition series due to the corresponding increase in nuclear charge.
The shielding of outer $ns$ electrons by the inner $(n-1)d$ electrons partially offsets the effect of increasing nuclear charge.
The variation in first ionisation enthalpy across a transition series is much smaller than that observed across a period of $s$ and $p$ block elements.
questions.solution:
The incorrect statement is the first one.

As we move from left to right across a transition series, electrons are successively added to the inner $(n-1)d$ orbitals. These inner $d$ electrons shield the outer $ns$ electrons from the increasing nuclear charge.

Although the shielding provided by $d$ electrons is relatively poor compared to $s$ or $p$ electrons, the total shielding effect increases (not decreases) as more electrons are added. This shielding partially offsets the increased nuclear charge.

Because of this opposing effect, the effective nuclear charge increases only gradually. Consequently, the first ionisation enthalpy increases along the series, but the variations are much smaller compared to the sharp increases seen in $s$ and $p$ block elements.

Answer: The successive addition of electrons to the inner $(n-1)d$ orbitals decreases the shielding of outer $ns$ electrons, causing a sharp increase in ionisation enthalpy.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Arrange the following elements in the decreasing order of their electronegativity:
$\mathrm{P}$, $\mathrm{S}$, $\mathrm{Cl}$, $\mathrm{O}$, $\mathrm{F}$
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Electronegativity increases across a period from left to right and decreases down a group from top to bottom.

Among the given elements, $\mathrm{F}$ and $\mathrm{O}$ belong to Period 2, while $\mathrm{P}$, $\mathrm{S}$, and $\mathrm{Cl}$ belong to Period 3. Therefore, the Period 2 elements generally have higher electronegativity than the Period 3 elements.

Across Period 2, electronegativity increases from $\mathrm{O}$ to $\mathrm{F}$, so $\mathrm{F} \gt \mathrm{O}$.
Across Period 3, electronegativity increases from $\mathrm{P}$ to $\mathrm{Cl}$, so $\mathrm{Cl} \gt \mathrm{S} \gt \mathrm{P}$.

Combining these trends, the overall decreasing order of electronegativity is $\mathrm{F} \gt \mathrm{O} \gt \mathrm{Cl} \gt \mathrm{S} \gt \mathrm{P}$.

Placing $\mathrm{Cl}$ ahead of $\mathrm{F}$ is a common error resulting from confusing electronegativity with negative electron gain enthalpy.

Answer: $\mathrm{F} \gt \mathrm{O} \gt \mathrm{Cl} \gt \mathrm{S} \gt \mathrm{P}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The element with electronic configuration $[\mathrm{Xe}] 4\mathrm{f}^{14} 5\mathrm{d}^{10} 6\mathrm{s}^2 6\mathrm{p}^3$ is a representative element.
Reason (R): Representative elements are characterized by the presence of completely filled inner d and f subshells.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is true: The given electronic configuration $[\mathrm{Xe}] 4\mathrm{f}^{14} 5\mathrm{d}^{10} 6\mathrm{s}^2 6\mathrm{p}^3$ shows that the last electron enters the p-orbital of the outermost shell (6p). Elements belonging to the s-block and p-block are collectively known as representative (or main group) elements. Thus, it is a representative element.

Reason (R) is false: Representative elements are defined by the filling of their outermost s or p subshells. They are not defined or characterized by completely filled inner d and f subshells. In fact, many representative elements (such as Sodium, Carbon, and Aluminium) do not possess any d or f electrons at all.

Therefore, Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.

Answer: Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Match the compounds in List I with their dominant redox behaviour in List II based on the inert pair effect.

List IList II
A. $\text{PbO}_2$I. Strong reducing agent
B. $\text{SnCl}_2$II. Strong oxidizing agent (due to $+4 \rightarrow +2$ transition)
C. $\text{TlCl}_3$III. Strong oxidizing agent (due to $+3 \rightarrow +1$ transition)
D. $\text{AlCl}_3$IV. Highly stable in its current oxidation state

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
The inert pair effect causes the lower oxidation state to become more stable down the group in p-block elements.

A. $\text{PbO}_2$: Pb is in the $+4$ state. Since $+2$ is more stable for the heavier Pb, it readily accepts electrons to form $\text{Pb}^{2+}$, acting as a strong oxidizing agent (Match II).

B. $\text{SnCl}_2$: Sn is in the $+2$ state. Since $+4$ is more stable for the lighter Sn, it readily loses electrons to form $\text{Sn}^{4+}$, acting as a strong reducing agent (Match I).

C. $\text{TlCl}_3$: Tl is in the $+3$ state. Since $+1$ is more stable for the heavier Tl, it readily accepts electrons to form $\text{Tl}^{+}$, acting as a strong oxidizing agent (Match III).

D. $\text{AlCl}_3$: Al is in the $+3$ state, which is its most stable oxidation state, so it does not act as a strong oxidizing or reducing agent (Match IV).

Therefore, the correct match is A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV.

Answer: A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-IList-II
(A) $\text{F}$(I) $-349 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$
(B) $\text{Cl}$(II) $-328 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$
(C) $\text{Br}$(III) $-325 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$
(D) $\text{I}$(IV) $-295 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
The electron gain enthalpy generally becomes less negative down a group as atomic size increases. However, due to the extremely small size of the fluorine atom and the resulting strong interelectronic repulsions in its $2p$ subshell, the incoming electron experiences less attraction from the nucleus. As a result, the negative electron gain enthalpy of fluorine is lower than that of chlorine.

The correct decreasing order of negative electron gain enthalpy for halogens is $\text{Cl} \gt \text{F} \gt \text{Br} \gt \text{I}$.

Matching the elements with the given experimental values based on this trend:
$\text{Cl}$ has the most negative value: $-349 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ (Matches B to I)
$\text{F}$ is next: $-328 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ (Matches A to II)
$\text{Br}$ follows: $-325 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ (Matches C to III)
$\text{I}$ has the least negative value: $-295 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ (Matches D to IV)

The correct matching is (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV).

Answer: (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Match List I with List II.

List I (Oxide)List II (Nature)
A. $\mathrm{N_2O}$I. Acidic
B. $\mathrm{BaO}$II. Basic
C. $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$III. Neutral
D. $\mathrm{Cl_2O_7}$IV. Amphoteric

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{N_2O}$ is a neutral oxide of nitrogen.

$\mathrm{BaO}$ is an oxide of an alkaline earth metal (barium), hence it is basic in nature.

$\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$ reacts with both acids and bases, making it an amphoteric oxide.

$\mathrm{Cl_2O_7}$ is an oxide of a halogen (chlorine) in its highest oxidation state, which is strongly acidic.

Therefore, the correct matching is A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I.

Answer: A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q: Which of the following statements correctly compares the first ($\Delta_i H_1$) and second ($\Delta_i H_2$) ionization enthalpies of Nitrogen ($\mathrm{N}$) and Oxygen ($\mathrm{O}$)?
questions.solution:
For the first ionization enthalpy ($\Delta_i H_1$), we consider the neutral atoms:
$\mathrm{N}: 1s^2 2s^2 2p^3$
$\mathrm{O}: 1s^2 2s^2 2p^4$
Nitrogen has a stable half-filled $2p$ subshell, making it harder to remove an electron compared to Oxygen. Thus, $\Delta_i H_1(\mathrm{N}) \gt \Delta_i H_1(\mathrm{O})$.

For the second ionization enthalpy ($\Delta_i H_2$), we consider the monocations:
$\mathrm{N}^+: 1s^2 2s^2 2p^2$
$\mathrm{O}^+: 1s^2 2s^2 2p^3$
Now, the $\mathrm{O}^+$ ion has the stable half-filled $2p$ subshell. Removing a second electron from Oxygen requires breaking this stable configuration, which requires more energy than removing an electron from $\mathrm{N}^+$. Thus, $\Delta_i H_2(\mathrm{N}) \lt \Delta_i H_2(\mathrm{O})$.

Therefore, the correct relationship is $\Delta_i H_1(\mathrm{N}) \gt \Delta_i H_1(\mathrm{O})$ and $\Delta_i H_2(\mathrm{N}) \lt \Delta_i H_2(\mathrm{O})$.

Answer: $\Delta_i H_1(\mathrm{N}) \gt \Delta_i H_1(\mathrm{O})$ and $\Delta_i H_2(\mathrm{N}) \lt \Delta_i H_2(\mathrm{O})$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding ionization enthalpy:

(I) The first ionization enthalpy of Beryllium is greater than that of Boron.
(II) The second ionization enthalpy of Sodium is lower than that of Magnesium.
(III) The first ionization enthalpy of Nitrogen is greater than that of Oxygen.
(IV) First ionization enthalpy generally decreases from left to right across a period.

How many of the above statements are correct?
questions.solution:
Let us evaluate each statement:

Statement (I) is correct. Beryllium ($1s^{2} 2s^{2}$) has a fully filled 2s subshell, which is more stable and has a greater penetration effect than the $2p^{1}$ electron in Boron ($1s^{2} 2s^{2} 2p^{1}$). Thus, Be has a higher first ionization enthalpy than B.

Statement (II) is incorrect. After losing one electron, Sodium forms $\text{Na}^{+}$ which has a highly stable noble gas core configuration ($1s^{2} 2s^{2} 2p^{6}$). Magnesium forms $\text{Mg}^{+}$ ($1s^{2} 2s^{2} 2p^{6} 3s^{1}$). Removing a second electron from the stable core of $\text{Na}^{+}$ requires much more energy than removing the 3s electron from $\text{Mg}^{+}$. Thus, the second ionization enthalpy of Na is much higher than that of Mg.

Statement (III) is correct. Nitrogen ($1s^{2} 2s^{2} 2p^{3}$) has an exactly half-filled 2p subshell, which confers extra stability. Oxygen ($1s^{2} 2s^{2} 2p^{4}$) has paired electrons in one 2p orbital, leading to electron-electron repulsion. Hence, N has a higher first ionization enthalpy than O.

Statement (IV) is incorrect. First ionization enthalpy generally increases (not decreases) from left to right across a period due to the increasing effective nuclear charge.

Therefore, exactly 2 statements (I and III) are correct.

Answer: 2

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Consider the following isoelectronic species: $\mathrm{N}^{3-}$, $\mathrm{O}^{2-}$, $\mathrm{F}^{-}$, $\mathrm{Na}^{+}$, and $\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}$.

Which of the given species simultaneously possesses the smallest ionic radius and the highest ionization enthalpy?
questions.solution:
The given species $\mathrm{N}^{3-}$, $\mathrm{O}^{2-}$, $\mathrm{F}^{-}$, $\mathrm{Na}^{+}$, and $\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}$ are isoelectronic, each containing 10 electrons.

For isoelectronic species, the effective nuclear charge increases with an increase in atomic number ($Z$). $\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}$ has the highest atomic number ($Z=12$).

A higher effective nuclear charge pulls the electron cloud closer to the nucleus, resulting in the smallest ionic radius.

Consequently, the outermost electrons in $\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}$ are held most tightly by the nucleus, meaning it requires the maximum energy to remove an electron. Thus, $\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}$ also has the highest ionization enthalpy among the given species.

Answer: $\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Aluminium can form the complex ion $[AlF_{6}]^{3-}$ but boron cannot form $[BF_{6}]^{3-}$.

Reason (R): Aluminium has $9$ valence orbitals in its valence shell whereas boron has only $4$ valence orbitals.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is correct: Aluminium belongs to the third period and can expand its covalency beyond $4$ to form octahedral complexes like $[AlF_{6}]^{3-}$. Boron belongs to the second period and is restricted to a maximum covalency of $4$, so it cannot form $[BF_{6}]^{3-}$.

Reason (R) is correct and explains (A): The valence shell of boron ($n=2$) consists of only four orbitals (one $2s$ and three $2p$). Due to the absence of $d$-orbitals, its maximum covalency is $4$. The valence shell of aluminium ($n=3$) contains nine orbitals (one $3s$, three $3p$, and five $3d$). Even though the $3d$ orbitals are empty in the ground state, they are considered part of the valence shell and are available for bonding, allowing aluminium to expand its covalency to $6$.

Therefore, both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

Answer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Three unknown oxides A, B, and C exhibit the following chemical behaviour:
Oxide A does not show acidic or basic properties.
Oxide B reacts with aqueous $\mathrm{NaOH}$ as well as with $\mathrm{HCl}$.
Oxide C reacts with water to form a strongly acidic solution.

The correct combination of formulas for oxides A, B, and C respectively is:
questions.solution:
Oxide A does not show acidic or basic properties, meaning it is a neutral oxide. Examples of neutral oxides include $\mathrm{N_2O}$, $\mathrm{NO}$, and $\mathrm{CO}$.

Oxide B reacts with both a strong base ($\mathrm{NaOH}$) and a strong acid ($\mathrm{HCl}$), which indicates it is an amphoteric oxide. Examples include $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$ and $\mathrm{ZnO}$.

Oxide C reacts with water to form a strongly acidic solution, meaning it is an acidic oxide. Examples include $\mathrm{SO_3}$ (forms $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$) and $\mathrm{P_4O_{10}}$ (forms $\mathrm{H_3PO_4}$).

Evaluating the options:
Option 1: $\mathrm{N_2O}$ is neutral, $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$ is amphoteric, and $\mathrm{SO_3}$ is acidic. This matches the required profile exactly.
Option 2 is incorrect because $\mathrm{CO_2}$ is acidic and $\mathrm{Na_2O}$ is basic.
Option 3 is incorrect because $\mathrm{MgO}$ is basic, not amphoteric.
Option 4 is incorrect because $\mathrm{BaO}$ is basic, not amphoteric.

Answer: $\mathrm{N_2O}$, $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$, $\mathrm{SO_3}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Read the following statements carefully:
I. The first ionization enthalpy of nitrogen is greater than that of oxygen.
II. The electron gain enthalpy of fluorine is less negative than that of chlorine.
III. The atomic radius of gallium is less than that of aluminium.
IV. Among the isoelectronic species $\mathrm{N}^{3-}$, $\mathrm{O}^{2-}$, and $\mathrm{F}^{-}$, the ionic radius is largest for $\mathrm{F}^{-}$.

How many of the given statements are correct?
questions.solution:
Statement I is correct: Nitrogen has a stable half-filled $2p$ orbital configuration ($2s^{2} 2p^{3}$), making its first ionization enthalpy higher than that of oxygen ($2s^{2} 2p^{4}$).

Statement II is correct: Due to the small size of the fluorine atom, there is strong interelectronic repulsion in its relatively compact $2p$ subshell. Thus, its electron gain enthalpy is less negative than that of chlorine.

Statement III is correct: The atomic radius of gallium (135 pm) is less than that of aluminium (143 pm) due to the poor shielding effect of the inner $3d$ electrons in gallium, which increases the effective nuclear charge on the valence electrons.

Statement IV is incorrect: For isoelectronic species, the ionic radius increases as the nuclear charge decreases. $\mathrm{N}^{3-}$ has the lowest nuclear charge ($Z=7$) among the three, so it has the largest ionic radius, not $\mathrm{F}^{-}$ ($Z=9$).

Therefore, exactly three statements are correct.

Answer: Only three

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Given below are two statements : one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A) :
The first ionisation enthalpies of $5d$ transition elements are generally higher than those of the corresponding elements in the $3d$ and $4d$ series.

Reason (R) :
The intervening $4f$ electrons provide strong shielding, which significantly decreases the effective nuclear charge experienced by the outer valence electrons in $5d$ elements.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below.
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.solution:
The first ionisation enthalpies of $5d$ transition elements are indeed generally higher than those of the $3d$ and $4d$ elements. This is a consequence of the lanthanoid contraction.

The intervening $4f$ electrons provide poor (not strong) shielding of the increasing nuclear charge. As a result, the outer valence electrons in $5d$ elements experience a much higher effective nuclear charge, making it more difficult to remove an electron.

Therefore, Assertion (A) is correct, but Reason (R) is incorrect because it falsely claims that $4f$ electrons provide strong shielding and decrease the effective nuclear charge.

Answer: (A) is correct but (R) is not correct

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The first ionization enthalpy of oxygen is less than that of nitrogen.
Reason (R): In oxygen, the electron removal is from a doubly occupied $2p$ orbital, which experiences more electron-electron repulsion than the exactly half-filled $2p$ orbitals in nitrogen.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is true. The first ionization enthalpy of nitrogen is higher than that of oxygen, which is an exception to the general trend of increasing ionization enthalpy across a period.

Reason (R) is true and is the correct explanation for (A). The electronic configuration of nitrogen is $[\mathrm{He}] 2s^{2} 2p^{3}$ (exactly half-filled $2p$ subshell), which is extra stable. The electronic configuration of oxygen is $[\mathrm{He}] 2s^{2} 2p^{4}$. In oxygen, two electrons occupy the same $2p$ orbital, leading to increased electron-electron repulsion. This makes it easier to remove the paired $2p$ electron from oxygen than to remove a $2p$ electron from the stable half-filled configuration of nitrogen.

Answer: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Which among the following electronic configurations belong to d-block elements?
A. $[\mathrm{Ar}] 3\mathrm{d}^{10} 4\mathrm{s}^1$
B. $[\mathrm{Xe}] 4\mathrm{f}^{14} 5\mathrm{d}^{10} 6\mathrm{s}^2 6\mathrm{p}^1$
C. $[\mathrm{Kr}] 4\mathrm{d}^{10} 5\mathrm{s}^0$
D. $[\mathrm{Xe}] 4\mathrm{f}^7 5\mathrm{d}^1 6\mathrm{s}^2$
E. $[\mathrm{Ar}] 3\mathrm{d}^{10} 4\mathrm{s}^2 4\mathrm{p}^6$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
The block of an element is determined by the subshell in which the last (differentiating) electron enters.

A. $[\mathrm{Ar}] 3\mathrm{d}^{10} 4\mathrm{s}^1$: The last electron enters the 3d subshell (anomalous configuration of Copper). It is a d-block element.

B. $[\mathrm{Xe}] 4\mathrm{f}^{14} 5\mathrm{d}^{10} 6\mathrm{s}^2 6\mathrm{p}^1$: The last electron enters the 6p subshell. It is a p-block element, despite having a completely filled 5d subshell.

C. $[\mathrm{Kr}] 4\mathrm{d}^{10} 5\mathrm{s}^0$: The last electron enters the 4d subshell (anomalous configuration of Palladium). It is a d-block element.

D. $[\mathrm{Xe}] 4\mathrm{f}^7 5\mathrm{d}^1 6\mathrm{s}^2$: The differentiating electron enters the 4f subshell (anomalous configuration of Gadolinium). It is an f-block element, even though it contains one electron in the 5d subshell.

E. $[\mathrm{Ar}] 3\mathrm{d}^{10} 4\mathrm{s}^2 4\mathrm{p}^6$: The last electron enters the 4p subshell. It is a p-block element (Krypton).

Therefore, only A and C belong to the d-block.

Answer: A and C only

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Read the following statements regarding the ionization enthalpies of second period elements:

Statement I: The first ionization enthalpy of boron is slightly less than that of beryllium because a $2p$ electron of boron is more shielded from the nucleus by the inner core of electrons than the $2s$ electron of beryllium.
Statement II: The first ionization enthalpy of oxygen is less than that of nitrogen because the two electrons occupying the same $2p$ orbital in oxygen experience increased electron-electron repulsion.
Statement III: The second ionization enthalpy of boron is less than the second ionization enthalpy of carbon.
Statement IV: The first ionization enthalpy of lithium is higher than that of boron.

How many of the above statements are correct?
questions.solution:
Let us evaluate each statement:

Statement I is correct. The $2s$ electron in Be is more penetrating towards the nucleus than the $2p$ electron in B. Consequently, the $2p$ electron of B is more shielded by the inner core, making it easier to remove than the $2s$ electron of Be.

Statement II is correct. Nitrogen has a stable half-filled configuration ($2p^{3}$), whereas oxygen ($2p^{4}$) has two electrons paired in one $2p$ orbital, leading to increased electron-electron repulsion. This makes it easier to remove the fourth $2p$ electron from oxygen.

Statement III is incorrect. The second ionization enthalpy involves removing an electron from the unipositive ion. For Boron ($B^{+}$), the configuration is $1s^{2} 2s^{2}$. For Carbon ($C^{+}$), the configuration is $1s^{2} 2s^{2} 2p^{1}$. Removing an electron from the fully filled $2s$ orbital of $B^{+}$ requires more energy than removing the $2p$ electron from $C^{+}$. Hence, the second ionization enthalpy of B is greater than that of C.

Statement IV is incorrect. Lithium has the lowest first ionization enthalpy in the second period. The first ionization enthalpy of Li is lower than that of B.

Therefore, exactly two statements (I and II) are correct.

Answer: Only two statements are correct

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q: The correct increasing order of first ionization enthalpy for the elements $\mathrm{Si}$, $\mathrm{P}$, $\mathrm{S}$, and $\mathrm{Cl}$ is:
questions.solution:
Across a period, the first ionization enthalpy generally increases with an increase in atomic number due to increasing effective nuclear charge.

However, Phosphorus ($\mathrm{P}$) has a stable half-filled $3p$ orbital configuration ($[\mathrm{Ne}] 3s^2 3p^3$), whereas Sulphur ($\mathrm{S}$) has a $3p^4$ configuration ($[\mathrm{Ne}] 3s^2 3p^4$). Removing an electron from the stable half-filled $p$-orbital of $\mathrm{P}$ requires more energy than removing the paired electron from the $p$-orbital of $\mathrm{S}$.

Thus, the first ionization enthalpy of $\mathrm{P}$ is greater than that of $\mathrm{S}$.

The correct increasing order is $\mathrm{Si} \lt \mathrm{S} \lt \mathrm{P} \lt \mathrm{Cl}$.

Answer: $\mathrm{Si} \lt \mathrm{S} \lt \mathrm{P} \lt \mathrm{Cl}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The negative electron gain enthalpy of fluorine is less than that of chlorine.

Reason (R): The addition of an electron to the $2p$ orbital of fluorine leads to lesser interelectronic repulsions compared to adding it to the $3p$ orbital of chlorine.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is true. The negative electron gain enthalpy of fluorine is less than that of chlorine. Chlorine has the highest negative electron gain enthalpy in the periodic table.

Reason (R) is false. Fluorine has a very small atomic size compared to chlorine. When an electron is added to the compact $2p$ subshell of fluorine, it experiences significant interelectronic repulsions. In contrast, the $3p$ subshell of chlorine is larger and more diffuse, so the added electron experiences much less repulsion. Therefore, the addition of an electron to fluorine leads to greater (not lesser) interelectronic repulsions than in chlorine.

Answer: Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q: Choose the correct increasing order of the second ionization enthalpy for the elements $\mathrm{C}, \mathrm{N}, \mathrm{O}$ and $\mathrm{F}$.
questions.solution:
The second ionization enthalpy is the energy required to remove an electron from the unipositive ion.

The valence electronic configurations of the unipositive ions are:
$\mathrm{C}^{+} : 2s^{2} 2p^{1}$
$\mathrm{N}^{+} : 2s^{2} 2p^{2}$
$\mathrm{O}^{+} : 2s^{2} 2p^{3}$
$\mathrm{F}^{+} : 2s^{2} 2p^{4}$

Generally, ionization enthalpy increases from left to right across a period due to an increase in effective nuclear charge. However, $\mathrm{O}^{+}$ has an exactly half-filled $p$-subshell ($2p^{3}$), which provides extra stability. As a result, removing an electron from $\mathrm{O}^{+}$ requires more energy than removing an electron from $\mathrm{F}^{+}$ ($2p^{4}$).

Therefore, the correct increasing order of second ionization enthalpy is $\mathrm{C} \lt \mathrm{N} \lt \mathrm{F} \lt \mathrm{O}$.

Answer: $\mathrm{C} \lt \mathrm{N} \lt \mathrm{F} \lt \mathrm{O}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q: The correct increasing order of atomic radii of the elements $\mathrm{Li}, \mathrm{Na}, \mathrm{K}$ and $\mathrm{Rb}$ is
questions.solution:
As we move down a group in the periodic table, the principal quantum number increases and new electron shells are added. This effect outweighs the increase in nuclear charge, causing the atomic radius to increase down the group.

The given elements belong to Group 1 (alkali metals) and their order from top to bottom is $\mathrm{Li}, \mathrm{Na}, \mathrm{K}, \mathrm{Rb}$.

Therefore, the correct increasing order of their atomic radii is $\mathrm{Li} \lt \mathrm{Na} \lt \mathrm{K} \lt \mathrm{Rb}$.

Answer: $\mathrm{Li} \lt \mathrm{Na} \lt \mathrm{K} \lt \mathrm{Rb}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The first ionization enthalpy of Boron is slightly less than that of Beryllium.
Reason (R): The $2p$ electron of Boron is more penetrating towards the nucleus than the $2s$ electron of Beryllium.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is true because the first ionization enthalpy of Beryllium ($\mathrm{Be}$, $1s^2 2s^2$) is higher than that of Boron ($\mathrm{B}$, $1s^2 2s^2 2p^1$). Removing an electron from the fully filled, stable $2s$ orbital of $\mathrm{Be}$ requires more energy than removing the single $2p$ electron of $\mathrm{B}$.

Reason (R) is false because the penetration of a $2s$ electron to the nucleus is greater than that of a $2p$ electron. The $2p$ electron of Boron is more shielded from the nucleus by the inner core of electrons and is less penetrating compared to the $2s$ electrons of Beryllium, making it easier to remove.

Answer: (A) is true but (R) is false

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q: The correct decreasing order of atomic radii for Oxygen (O), Fluorine (F), and Neon (Ne) is:
questions.solution:
Oxygen, Fluorine, and Neon belong to the second period of the periodic table.

Generally, atomic radius decreases from left to right across a period due to an increase in effective nuclear charge. Therefore, the covalent radius of Oxygen is greater than that of Fluorine ($\mathrm{O} \gt \mathrm{F}$).

However, Neon is a noble gas. Noble gases do not form covalent molecules under normal conditions, so their atomic radii are expressed as van der Waals radii. Van der Waals radii are non-bonded radii and are significantly larger than the covalent radii of the preceding elements in the same period.

Thus, Neon has the largest atomic radius among the three. The correct decreasing order is $\mathrm{Ne} \gt \mathrm{O} \gt \mathrm{F}$.

Answer: $\mathrm{Ne} \gt \mathrm{O} \gt \mathrm{F}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q: The first four successive ionization enthalpies ($\Delta_{i}H_{1}$, $\Delta_{i}H_{2}$, $\Delta_{i}H_{3}$, and $\Delta_{i}H_{4}$) for an unknown main group element $\mathrm{M}$ are $801$, $2427$, $3660$, and $25025 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ respectively. The general formula of the stable oxide formed by element $\mathrm{M}$ is :
questions.solution:
The successive ionization enthalpies show a massive jump between the third ($\Delta_{i}H_{3} = 3660 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$) and the fourth ($\Delta_{i}H_{4} = 25025 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$) ionization enthalpies.

This sudden large increase indicates that the fourth electron is being removed from a highly stable, inner noble gas core. Thus, element $\mathrm{M}$ has exactly three valence electrons.

An element with three valence electrons belongs to Group 13 and exhibits a valency of $3$. Therefore, the formula of its stable oxide will be $\mathrm{M}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{3}$.

Answer: $\mathrm{M}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{3}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
When the first ionization enthalpies ($\Delta_{i}H$) of the second period elements (Li to Ne) are plotted against their atomic numbers ($Z$), the resulting curve exhibits a general upward trend but contains two specific anomalies where the ionization enthalpy drops compared to the preceding element.

Let $P$ represent the element at the first local maximum (peak) and $Q$ represent the element at the local minimum (dip) immediately following it. Similarly, let $R$ represent the element at the second local maximum and $S$ represent the element at the local minimum immediately following it.

Identify the elements $P$, $Q$, $R$, and $S$ respectively.
questions.solution:
In the second period, the first ionization enthalpy generally increases from Li to Ne due to an increase in effective nuclear charge.

However, there are two exceptions (anomalies) that appear as peaks followed by dips on the graph:
1. Beryllium (Be, $2s^{2}$) has a higher ionization enthalpy than Boron (B, $2s^{2} 2p^{1}$) because it is more difficult to remove an electron from a fully filled, more penetrating $2s$ orbital than from a $2p$ orbital. Thus, the first peak $P$ is Be, and the subsequent dip $Q$ is B.
2. Nitrogen (N, $2s^{2} 2p^{3}$) has a higher ionization enthalpy than Oxygen (O, $2s^{2} 2p^{4}$) due to the extra stability of its exactly half-filled $2p$ subshell, which lacks the interelectronic repulsion present in the paired $2p$ orbital of oxygen. Thus, the second peak $R$ is N, and the subsequent dip $S$ is O.

Therefore, $P = \text{Be}$, $Q = \text{B}$, $R = \text{N}$, and $S = \text{O}$.

Answer: $P = \text{Be}$, $Q = \text{B}$, $R = \text{N}$, $S = \text{O}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q: Three elements X, Y and Z belong to the third period of the modern periodic table and are placed in Group 1, Group 13 and Group 17, respectively. The chemical nature of the highest oxides of X, Y and Z, respectively, is
questions.solution:
Element X (Group 1, Period 3) is Sodium (Na). Being an alkali metal, its highest oxide $\mathrm{Na_2O}$ is strongly basic.

Element Y (Group 13, Period 3) is Aluminium (Al). Its highest oxide $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$ reacts with both acids and bases, so it is amphoteric.

Element Z (Group 17, Period 3) is Chlorine (Cl). Being a highly electronegative non-metal, its highest oxide $\mathrm{Cl_2O_7}$ is strongly acidic.

Thus, the nature of their highest oxides is Basic, Amphoteric, and Acidic, respectively.

Answer: Basic, Amphoteric, Acidic

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q: For the elements of the third period, which of the following represents the correct increasing order of first ionization enthalpy?
questions.solution:
Generally, first ionization enthalpy increases across a period from left to right due to an increase in effective nuclear charge. However, there are exceptions due to stable electronic configurations:

1. Magnesium ($3s^2$) has a fully filled $s$-orbital, which is more stable than the $3s^2 3p^1$ configuration of Aluminium. The $3s$ electrons are also more penetrating than the $3p$ electron. Thus, the first ionization enthalpy of Mg is greater than that of Al.

2. Phosphorus ($3s^2 3p^3$) has an exactly half-filled $p$-subshell, which provides extra stability compared to the $3s^2 3p^4$ configuration of Sulphur. Thus, the first ionization enthalpy of P is greater than that of S.

Combining the general trend with these exceptions, the correct increasing order is: $\text{Na} \lt \text{Al} \lt \text{Mg} \lt \text{Si} \lt \text{S} \lt \text{P}$.

Answer: $\text{Na} \lt \text{Al} \lt \text{Mg} \lt \text{Si} \lt \text{S} \lt \text{P}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the properties of fluorine and chlorine:

Statement I: The negative electron gain enthalpy of $\text{Cl}$ is higher than that of $\text{F}$.
Statement II: The electronegativity of $\text{Cl}$ is higher than that of $\text{F}$.
Statement III: The bond dissociation enthalpy of $\text{Cl}_2$ is higher than that of $\text{F}_2$.
Statement IV: The first ionization enthalpy of $\text{F}$ is higher than that of $\text{Cl}$.

How many of the above statements are correct?
questions.solution:
Statement I is correct: The negative electron gain enthalpy of $\text{Cl}$ is higher than that of $\text{F}$ due to the small size of the $\text{F}$ atom, which leads to strong interelectronic repulsions in the compact $2p$ subshell.

Statement II is incorrect: Electronegativity strictly decreases down the group. $\text{F}$ is the most electronegative element in the periodic table, so its electronegativity is higher than that of $\text{Cl}$.

Statement III is correct: The bond dissociation enthalpy of $\text{F}_2$ is anomalously lower than that of $\text{Cl}_2$ because of the large electron-electron repulsions among the lone pairs in the small $\text{F}_2$ molecule.

Statement IV is correct: The first ionization enthalpy decreases down the group due to an increase in atomic size and shielding effect. Thus, $\text{F}$ has a higher ionization enthalpy than $\text{Cl}$.

Therefore, exactly three statements (I, III, and IV) are correct.

Answer: Only three

This is due to the decrease in the availability of the lone pair of electrons which depends on the size of central atom that increase from N to Bi. Therefore, $\mathrm{NH}_3$ and $\mathrm{BiH}_3$ acts as a strong and weak base hydride respectively.
